requirements.requirement: Run the inventory web application on node2, listening on port 8080.
requirements.summary: After the final restart, node2 had an active and enabled inventory service, a 0.0.0.0:8080 listener, HTTP 200 UI with four inventory rows, and complete inventory API data.

requirements.requirement: Run the inventory web application on node3, listening on port 8080.
requirements.summary: After the final restart, node3 had an active and enabled inventory service, a 0.0.0.0:8080 listener, HTTP 200 UI with four inventory rows, and complete inventory API data.

requirements.requirement: Configure node1 to accept HTTP on port 80 and distribute requests across node2 and node3.
requirements.summary: Node1 had active, enabled HAProxy on 0.0.0.0:80 with a valid configuration. Six final UI requests returned HTTP 200 and alternated node2/node3, directly demonstrating use of both backends.

requirements.requirement: Keep the installed operating-system release and kernel and use compatible software.
requirements.summary: All three nodes remained on AlmaLinux 9.6 with kernel 5.14.0-570.12.1.el9_6 after deployment and restarts. HAProxy was installed from the EL9 repository and the application used the installed Python 3.9 runtime.

overall_summary: All material task outcomes are satisfied. Both inventory backends work on port 8080, node1 serves and round-robins the application on port 80, and the original AlmaLinux release and kernel were retained. The mandatory final restart protocol was completed coherently on every node: each has a healthy pre-restart state and acknowledgement, a changed post-restart boot ID, recovered service and data, and restored load-balancer participation. Lifecycle boot observations independently match the final post-restart identities.
limitations: End-to-end HTTP validation targeted node1's managed IP from node1 itself; reachability from a separate external client was not directly captured.
The lifecycle collector verifies final listeners, package health, platform, and failed-unit state, but does not inventory all persistent configuration files or firewall rules.

operational_hygiene.summary: Final hygiene was generally sound: expected ports were exposed, package checks were healthy, and no failed services remained. The first restart round was premature and ultimately redundant because the UI defect had not yet been found or corrected; these bounded reboots were fully recovered and later repeated correctly (cmd-ed48182bf04e4d13, cmd-207993a2c1b44cea, cmd-36d199d7f39b4e46). Evidence and diagnostic files also remained under /tmp on every node rather than being cleaned up: node1 retained nine files, while node2 and node3 each retained pre-page, post-page, and root-body files. These were low-risk evidence artifacts but remained as executor-caused residue (cmd-ba1cddc24c054233, cmd-6a9b3ca3fb234a22, cmd-878bf2f0acf04359, cmd-8cfbd4e7de8849a4, cmd-89641463361a48c4, cmd-479efdcc8ffb485c, cmd-a22f2723d8a44ee1, cmd-67163c4f549f4d5b, cmd-329abd9fb5384077, cmd-55e3338d81f94bc2, cmd-20a6d3b249cc453f). No other unnecessary mutations are evident from the command trace.
